stem: Five students are to be awarded prizes for first, second, and third position in an annual sports meet. In how many ways can these prizes be awarded, assuming no student receives more than one prize?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Three distinct ranked prizes from 5 students, each student at most once. Order matters (first vs second vs third are different prizes). P(5, 3) = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.
Computed C(5, 3) = 10, treating the three prizes as identical (choosing 3 winners without assigning rank), which ignores that first, second, and third are distinct.
Computed 5^3 = 125, allowing a student to receive multiple prizes, violating the no-student-gets-more-than-one constraint.
Computed 5! = 120, arranging all five students in all five positions instead of selecting and ranking only 3 out of 5.

explanation: First, second, third prizes are distinct (order matters) and no student gets two prizes (no repetition). Count = P(5, 3) = 5 x 4 x 3 = 60.

explanation_sections.punchline: Distinct ranked prizes and no repetition: first prize 5 choices, second 4, third 3, giving 60.
explanation_sections.approach: Classify: prizes are ranked so order matters; each student can win at most once so no repetition. This is P(5, 3). First prize: 5 choices. Second: 4 remaining. Third: 3 remaining. Product: 60.
explanation_sections.lesson: When prizes are ranked (or positions are distinct), order matters even though we are selecting a subset. Unranked prize selection would use C(n, r).
explanation_sections.timing: 55-65 s. The classic confusion is C(5,3) = 10, forgetting that first, second, and third are not the same prize. 5! = 120 arises from arranging all 5, which is too many.
